Was the daughter murdered by someone?

The daughter died of illness, and her body was buried in the forest ground where the villagers bury their dead. A brown bear dug up the grave and was eating her corpse when the father found it. The father understood that the bear had not hunted a living person—wary brown bears rarely attack living humans—but had been drawn to the buried body and scavenged it. Because the villagers' relatives are buried in that same forest ground, the father now fears that bears will likewise dig up and eat other villagers' buried relatives; the horror is grave desecration by scavenging bears, not attacks on the living.

Was the daughter buried in a location apart from where other villagers are buried—so the father's fear is that the bear learned to associate burial places with food and may seek out the villagers' graves too?

Is the missing element that the father himself was responsible for the burial being vulnerable—for example, he buried her improperly, so he feels the other villagers' relatives are at risk because of a shared practice he now recognizes as flawed?
Did the daughter die of a disease that also killed other villagers, so many graves are being dug up—meaning the father's fear is about an ongoing pattern, not just a possibility?
Did the disease that killed the daughter also kill other villagers?
Is the father's fear that bears will repeatedly dig up and eat the bodies of the many villagers who died of the disease (not just his daughter's)?
Were villagers who died of the disease buried in the forest because there was no proper cemetery yet in this newly settled village, placing many fresh graves within reach of the bears?
Were villagers buried in the forest because that was the village's ordinary burial place/practice—not for lack of a cemetery and not because of the disease?
Were the disease victims buried in the forest specifically (away from the village) out of fear of the disease, even though normal burials would be elsewhere nearer the village?
Is burial in the forest the village's ordinary, normal burial practice?
Did the father's fear include that, because so many died of the disease and were buried in the forest, bears will be drawn to the many fresh graves and repeatedly disturb them?

A disease had swept the newly settled village and killed many people, including the father's only daughter; she was already dead when the bear found her. In this village it is the ordinary practice to bury the dead in the forest, so the daughter and the other disease victims were buried there, in the same burial ground where villagers' relatives lie. Brown bears are wary and rarely attack living humans, so this bear had not hunted her as prey—it had dug up her buried corpse and was scavenging it. Seeing this, the father realizes that the many fresh forest graves are within reach of scavenging bears, and he fears that bears will repeatedly dig up and eat the buried bodies of the other villagers' relatives, so that others in the village will suffer the same desecration of a loved one's remains.
Does the father fear that living villagers will be killed and eaten by bears (as opposed to their buried bodies being eaten)?

Was the daughter not given the full normal burial preparation (such as cremation or proper rites) — perhaps only hastily buried because of the disease — leaving her body unusually exposed to scavengers?
Have bears already been digging up and eating other villagers' graves besides the daughter's?
Is an important part of the answer that the village is newly settled in bear territory—so bears are numerous and close by, making the forest graves especially vulnerable to them?
Is grave-robbing by bears a known/common occurrence in this region, which is why the father immediately understands other villagers' graves are also at risk?
Are the other villagers' relatives buried in the same specific burial location as the father's daughter?
Was the daughter's grave freshly made (recent burial), and was it because the body/grave was fresh that the bear was attracted to dig it up?
Was the daughter's grave freshly made (a recent burial)?
Was the bear attracted to the grave specifically because the burial was fresh?
Does the father's fear specifically involve bears eating the buried bodies of other villagers' dead relatives?
Does the father fear that bears, having learned that graves contain food, will teach or spread this scavenging behavior so that more bears begin robbing graves?
Did the disease kill a large number of villagers (many, not just a few)?
Did the father's shot fail to kill the bear (it escaped or he only wounded it), so the same grave-robbing bear remains a threat?
Was the daughter buried by the villagers (community) in the forest as part of the ordinary funeral procedure, without any special or unusual choice being made?

The father's daughter had died (of illness), and like other villagers she was given the ordinary funeral: burial in the forest, where the village's dead—including other villagers' relatives—lie. A brown bear dug up her grave and was eating the buried corpse when the father found it. Since these wary bears rarely attack living humans, the father understands the bear was not hunting a living person but scavenging a buried body. He therefore realizes that the same forest burial ground leaves other villagers' dead relatives vulnerable, and he fears that bears will likewise dig up and eat their buried loved ones.

Is an additional part of the father's fear that the forest burial ground will become unusable—villagers can no longer safely bury their dead there—so the community's way of burying relatives is threatened?
Did the daughter actually die of illness/disease (not merely the father's mistaken belief)?
Is the father's fear that villagers who die in the future will have their bodies dug up and eaten by bears?

The daughter died of illness and received the village's ordinary funeral: burial in the forest, the ground where other villagers' relatives are also buried. When the father found the brown bear, it had dug up her grave and was scavenging her buried corpse. These wary bears rarely attack living humans, so the father understood the bear had not hunted a living person but was eating a buried body. Because the villagers' relatives are buried in that same forest ground, he now fears that bears will dig up and eat those already-buried relatives' bodies—that other villagers will suffer the same desecration of a loved one's grave.
In this village's beliefs, is it significant or auspicious/inauspicious for a bear to eat human remains—connecting the father's fear to religious meaning rather than mere desecration?
Does the father's fear involve a food shortage, such that villagers may be driven to eat the bodies/meat of their own dead relatives?
Are there many bears in the area such that the father expects other bears to also raid the forest graves?
Was the daughter (or the village) previously familiar to the bear—had the bear been near the village or known to people before—so its eating her reflects a bear losing fear of these specific humans?
Is the village's forest burial ground located within the bears' natural habitat/territory, so that the buried dead are effectively left where bears live and forage?

The village follows the ordinary practice of burying its dead in a forest ground that lies within the bears' own habitat, where bears naturally roam and forage. The daughter died of illness and was buried there alongside other villagers' relatives. While foraging in its territory, a brown bear came upon her grave, dug up the buried corpse, and was eating it when the father found them. Because wary brown bears rarely attack living humans, the father understood the bear had not hunted a living person—it had simply found and scavenged a buried body lying in bear country. Since all the villagers' dead relatives are buried in that same ground within the bears' habitat, he fears those buried loved ones will likewise be found, dug up, and eaten by bears, so that other villagers will suffer as he has.
Are the village's dead ever left in the forest before burial (awaiting funeral rites or burial), so that waiting bodies—not only buried graves—are accessible to bears?
Is this the first/previously unheard-of case of a bear digging up a human grave in this area, so the father's fear stems from this being a new and spreading behavior?
Do the bears treat the human bodies buried in their forest habitat as an available food source, scavenging them opportunistically as they would other carrion in their territory?

The village's ordinary practice is to bury its dead in the forest, and that burial ground lies within the brown bears' habitat. The father's daughter died of illness and was buried there, as other villagers' relatives are. Bears wary of living humans still scavenge carrion in their territory, and a bear had dug up her grave and was eating the buried corpse when the father found it. Seeing this, the father realizes the village's dead are buried where bears forage—buried human bodies are simply food available to the bears. He therefore fears that the other villagers' relatives buried in that same ground will likewise be dug up and eaten by bears, so that others will suffer having a relative's body consumed.

The father's daughter died of illness and was buried according to the village's ordinary custom. Because the village buries its dead in a forest burial ground that lies within the brown bears' territory, and bears—though wary of living humans and rarely attacking them—readily scavenge carrion in their habitat, a bear dug up her grave and was eating her buried body when the father found it. The father understood that the bear had not hunted or killed a living person; it had merely found and consumed a buried body left in bear country. Knowing that all the villagers' relatives are buried in that same ground, and that human bodies buried there are effectively food available to the bears, he fears those other buried loved ones will likewise be dug up and eaten—so that other villagers will suffer the same horror and grief of having a relative's body consumed.
